primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: X-linked Alport syndrome due to COL4A5 pathogenic variant
mechanism: COL4A5 encodes the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen, a component of basement-membrane collagen networks; pathogenic variants disrupt the alpha3-alpha4-alpha5 type IV collagen network in the glomerular basement membrane and can also affect cochlear and ocular basement membranes.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus. His maternal uncle developed kidney failure at a young age. Molecular testing identifies a pathogenic variant in COL4A5.
lead: Which protein is directly encoded by the mutated gene in this patient?
correct: The alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen
distractors: The alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
The alpha-4 chain of type IV collagen
The alpha-1 chain of type I collagen
Fibrillin-1
distractor_notes: COL4A3 encodes the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen and can cause autosomal Alport syndromes, but it is not the gene identified in this stem.
COL4A4 encodes the alpha-4 chain of type IV collagen and can cause autosomal Alport syndromes, but it is not the gene identified in this stem.
Type I collagen alpha chains are encoded by COL1A genes and are associated with disorders such as osteogenesis imperfecta, not COL4A5-related Alport syndrome.
Fibrillin-1 is encoded by FBN1 and is associated with Marfan syndrome, not Alport syndrome.
key_expl: COL4A5 encodes collagen alpha-5(IV). X-linked Alport syndrome commonly results from pathogenic COL4A5 variants and affects the glomerular basement membrane, with characteristic renal, auditory, and ocular manifestations.
objective: Link COL4A5-related X-linked Alport syndrome to the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Activated factor XIII is a transglutaminase that covalently cross-links fibrin after fibrin formation, stabilizing the clot; factor XIII deficiency can cause significant delayed bleeding despite normal PT and aPTT because routine clotting times measure events before factor XIII-mediated cross-linking.
vignette: A child has recurrent delayed bleeding after minor trauma and a history of prolonged bleeding from the umbilical stump. Platelet count, prothrombin time, and activated partial thromboplastin time are normal.
lead: Which hemostatic step is most directly impaired in this disorder?
correct: Covalent cross-linking of fibrin strands after fibrin formation
distractors: Thrombin-mediated cleavage of fibrinogen to fibrin
Activation of factor X by the intrinsic tenase complex
Von Willebrand factor-mediated platelet adhesion to subendothelium
Gamma-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors
distractor_notes: Defective thrombin generation or fibrinogen cleavage would generally disturb earlier coagulation steps and can alter routine clotting tests; factor XIII acts after fibrin is formed.
Intrinsic-tenase defects such as factor VIII or IX deficiency typically prolong the aPTT.
Von Willebrand factor defects primarily impair platelet adhesion and may alter factor VIII levels; they do not explain the classic normal-PT/aPTT factor XIII pattern.
Defective gamma-carboxylation affects vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X and typically alters PT and/or aPTT rather than isolated post-fibrin clot stabilization.
key_expl: Factor XIII is the fibrin-stabilizing transglutaminase. It cross-links fibrin after the clot has formed, so severe deficiency can produce delayed bleeding while PT and aPTT remain normal.
objective: Recognize factor XIII deficiency as a defect of post-formation fibrin cross-linking that is not detected by routine PT/aPTT testing.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy type 1A due to PMP22 duplication
mechanism: The recurrent 1.5-Mb duplication at 17p11.2 that includes PMP22 increases PMP22 gene dosage and is the most common cause of CMT1A, an autosomal dominant demyelinating peripheral neuropathy.
vignette: A 17-year-old boy has slowly progressive distal leg weakness, pes cavus, reduced ankle reflexes, and mild distal sensory loss. His father has similar findings. Nerve-conduction studies show a diffuse demyelinating neuropathy with markedly slowed conduction velocities.
lead: Which genetic alteration is most likely responsible for this classic phenotype?
correct: A 1.5-Mb duplication at 17p11.2 that includes PMP22
distractors: A 1.5-Mb deletion at 17p11.2 that includes PMP22
A pathogenic variant in MFN2 causing an axonal neuropathy
A pathogenic variant in GJB1 causing X-linked CMT
A GAA-repeat expansion in FXN
distractor_notes: The reciprocal PMP22 deletion is the common cause of hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies rather than classic CMT1A.
MFN2 is a major cause of CMT2A, which is primarily axonal rather than the classic demyelinating CMT1A pattern.
GJB1 causes CMT1X and follows X-linked inheritance rather than the autosomal dominant PMP22-duplication pattern described.
FXN GAA-repeat expansions cause Friedreich ataxia, not classic demyelinating CMT1A.
key_expl: CMT1A is classically caused by a recurrent 1.5-Mb duplication at 17p11.2 containing PMP22. Increased PMP22 dosage disrupts peripheral myelin and produces an autosomal dominant demyelinating neuropathy.
objective: Associate classic autosomal dominant demyelinating CMT1A with PMP22 duplication at 17p11.2.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility due to abnormal RYR1-mediated calcium release
mechanism: Malignant hyperthermia most commonly reflects pathogenic RYR1 variants that permit uncontrolled calcium release from the skeletal-muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum after triggering anesthetics, producing sustained contraction and a hypermetabolic crisis.
vignette: Shortly after induction of general anesthesia with a volatile anesthetic and succinylcholine, a patient develops rapidly rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, generalized muscle rigidity, tachycardia, metabolic acidosis, and hyperthermia.
lead: Which intracellular event most directly drives this syndrome?
correct: Uncontrolled release of calcium from the skeletal-muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum through ryanodine receptors
distractors: Failure of acetylcholine release from motor-nerve terminals due to SNARE cleavage
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
Excessive calcium sequestration into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by SERCA pumps
Autoantibody-mediated loss of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors
distractor_notes: Presynaptic SNARE cleavage is the mechanism of botulinum toxin and causes flaccid paralysis, not anesthetic-triggered hypermetabolic rigidity.
Acetylcholinesterase inhibition causes cholinergic excess and does not explain malignant hyperthermia.
Malignant hyperthermia involves excessive cytosolic calcium from sarcoplasmic-reticulum release, not excessive sequestration by SERCA.
Postsynaptic nicotinic-receptor autoimmunity causes myasthenia gravis, not malignant hyperthermia.
key_expl: Triggering anesthetics can provoke uncontrolled RYR1-mediated calcium release from the skeletal-muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum in susceptible patients. Sustained contraction and ATP consumption produce the hypermetabolic crisis.
objective: Explain malignant hyperthermia as uncontrolled RYR1-mediated calcium release from skeletal-muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Holt-Oram syndrome is an autosomal dominant heart-hand syndrome caused by reduced TBX5 function and is characterized by preaxial radial-ray upper-limb anomalies together with cardiac septation defects and/or conduction disease.
vignette: A 9-year-old child has a hypoplastic thumb and shortened radius on one side. Echocardiography shows an ostium secundum atrial septal defect, and electrocardiography shows first-degree atrioventricular block. The lower limbs are normal, and the complete blood count is normal.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this combination of findings?
distractors: Thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome
Fanconi anemia
VACTERL association
Thalidomide embryopathy
distractor_notes: Thrombocytopenia-absent radius syndrome classically includes bilateral radial aplasia with thumbs present and thrombocytopenia, unlike this child with a normal blood count and a heart-conduction phenotype.
Fanconi anemia can include radial-ray abnormalities but is associated with bone-marrow failure and does not characteristically combine the specific heart-hand pattern with conduction disease.
VACTERL requires a broader constellation of vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb anomalies and does not specifically define the TBX5-associated radial-ray/conduction pattern.
Thalidomide embryopathy can cause limb-reduction defects but does not explain the inherited-style heart-hand syndrome with characteristic conduction disease.
key_expl: Holt-Oram syndrome combines preaxial radial-ray upper-limb abnormalities with cardiac septal defects and/or conduction disease. Pathogenic TBX5 variants are the major molecular cause.
objective: Recognize Holt-Oram syndrome from the combination of radial-ray upper-limb anomalies and cardiac septation/conduction abnormalities.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Hereditary fructose intolerance due to aldolase B deficiency
mechanism: Aldolase B deficiency prevents cleavage of fructose-1-phosphate into glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone phosphate; fructose-1-phosphate accumulates, traps phosphate, depletes ATP, and inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
vignette: An 8-month-old infant develops vomiting, lethargy, hypoglycemia, and hepatomegaly after fruit puree and juice are introduced. The infant becomes well when these foods are avoided and later strongly avoids sweet foods.
lead: Which metabolite accumulates directly because of the deficient enzyme in this disorder?
distractors: Fructose-6-phosphate
Galactose-1-phosphate
Sorbitol
Glucose-1-phosphate
distractor_notes: Fructose-6-phosphate is a glycolytic intermediate and is not the substrate that accumulates when aldolase B is deficient.
Galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in classic galactosemia due to GALT deficiency.
Sorbitol can accumulate in tissues during hyperglycemia through the polyol pathway but is not the defining metabolite of hereditary fructose intolerance.
Glucose-1-phosphate is generated during glycogenolysis and is not the direct substrate of aldolase B.
key_expl: Aldolase B normally cleaves fructose-1-phosphate. In hereditary fructose intolerance, fructose-1-phosphate accumulates after fructose exposure and contributes to phosphate depletion, ATP depletion, and inhibition of hepatic glucose production.
objective: Identify fructose-1-phosphate accumulation as the direct metabolic consequence of aldolase B deficiency in hereditary fructose intolerance.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: 17-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency due to CYP17A1 loss of function
mechanism: CYP17A1 deficiency impairs both cortisol and sex-steroid synthesis while diverting steroid precursors toward mineralocorticoid-active compounds such as deoxycorticosterone, producing hypertension, hypokalemia, and sexual infantilism.
vignette: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea and absent pubertal development. She has hypertension and hypokalemia, low plasma renin activity, low cortisol, and low androgen concentrations.
lead: Deficiency of which enzyme best explains this pattern?
distractors: 21-hydroxylase
11-beta-hydroxylase
Aromatase
5-alpha-reductase
distractor_notes: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes cortisol and often aldosterone deficiency with androgen excess, typically producing salt wasting and/or virilization rather than hypertension with low androgens.
11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency can cause hypertension through deoxycorticosterone excess but also causes androgen excess, which conflicts with absent pubertal development and low androgens.
Aromatase deficiency impairs estrogen synthesis and can cause virilization but does not produce the classic mineralocorticoid hypertension/hypokalemia pattern.
5-alpha-reductase deficiency affects conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in 46,XY individuals and does not explain this adrenal mineralocorticoid phenotype.
key_expl: 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency decreases cortisol and sex steroids while increasing mineralocorticoid-active precursors, producing hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin, and absent sexual maturation.
objective: Recognize CYP17A1 deficiency from hypertension/hypokalemia plus deficient cortisol and sex-steroid synthesis.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Zellweger spectrum disorder due to PEX-related peroxisome biogenesis defect
mechanism: PEX-gene defects impair peroxisome biogenesis and multiple peroxisomal pathways, including beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids; severe Zellweger spectrum disease can present in the newborn period with hypotonia, seizures, liver disease, renal cysts, and elevated VLCFAs.
vignette: A newborn has profound hypotonia, poor feeding, seizures, hepatomegaly, and renal cortical cysts. Plasma testing shows markedly elevated very-long-chain fatty acids, and molecular testing identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in PEX1.
lead: The abnormal plasma lipid profile most directly reflects failure of which metabolic process?
correct: Beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids in peroxisomes
distractors: Beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids in mitochondria
Lysosomal degradation of sphingomyelin
Cytosolic synthesis of fatty acids from acetyl-CoA
Mitochondrial oxidation of branched-chain amino acids
distractor_notes: Mitochondrial beta-oxidation defects can cause hypoketotic hypoglycemia and cardiomyopathy but do not explain the PEX1-associated peroxisome-biogenesis phenotype with VLCFA accumulation.
Lysosomal sphingomyelin degradation is impaired in acid sphingomyelinase deficiency, not Zellweger spectrum disorder.
Cytosolic fatty-acid synthesis does not account for the characteristic accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids from failed peroxisomal catabolism.
Branched-chain amino-acid oxidation is impaired in maple syrup urine disease and is unrelated to PEX-mediated peroxisome biogenesis.
key_expl: Peroxisomes are required for beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids. PEX-related peroxisome-biogenesis defects impair this pathway, causing elevated plasma VLCFAs in Zellweger spectrum disorder.
objective: Link Zellweger spectrum disorder to defective peroxisome biogenesis and impaired peroxisomal beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids.

diagnosis: Partial verification bias in a diagnostic-accuracy study
mechanism: Partial verification bias occurs when only a selected subset of participants who receive an index diagnostic test undergo the reference standard, often because verification is more likely after a positive index result, distorting estimates of diagnostic accuracy.
vignette: Investigators evaluate a new blood test for a disease. Every participant receives the new test, but the invasive reference-standard procedure is performed in all participants with a positive new test and in only a small nonrandom subset of those with a negative new test. Sensitivity and specificity are then estimated only among participants whose disease status was verified.
lead: Which bias most directly threatens the reported diagnostic accuracy?
distractors: Spectrum bias
Incorporation bias
Diagnostic review bias
Lead-time bias
distractor_notes: Spectrum bias arises when test performance differs because the study sample does not represent the relevant spectrum of disease and nondisease, not because reference-standard verification depends on the index result.
Incorporation bias occurs when the index test itself is included in the reference standard used to define disease status.
Diagnostic review bias occurs when interpretation of the reference standard is influenced by knowledge of the index-test result; the central defect here is selective verification.
Lead-time bias is a screening-survival artifact and is unrelated to selective application of a diagnostic reference standard.
key_expl: Only a selected subset receives the reference standard, with verification strongly influenced by the index-test result. This is partial verification, or work-up, bias and can distort sensitivity and specificity estimates.
objective: Identify partial verification bias when reference-standard confirmation is selectively performed after an index diagnostic test.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Menkes disease due to ATP7A loss of function
mechanism: ATP7A is a copper-transporting ATPase that supports intracellular copper delivery and copper efflux from enterocytes; loss of ATP7A traps copper in intestinal cells and produces systemic copper deficiency with impaired copper-dependent enzymes.
vignette: A 3-month-old boy has failure to thrive, hypotonia, seizures, and sparse, brittle, kinky hair. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin concentrations are low.
lead: Which transport defect most directly causes the systemic copper deficiency in this disorder?
correct: Impaired ATP7A-mediated copper efflux from intestinal enterocytes
distractors: Impaired ATP7B-mediated biliary copper excretion from hepatocytes
Impaired ferroportin-mediated iron export from enterocytes
Impaired intestinal uptake of heme iron through heme transport pathways
Excess intestinal copper absorption with defective hepatic storage
distractor_notes: ATP7B loss causes Wilson disease by reducing biliary copper excretion and promoting copper accumulation rather than systemic copper deficiency from intestinal trapping.
Ferroportin exports iron, not copper, from enterocytes.
Heme-iron uptake pathways do not explain the characteristic copper deficiency, kinky hair, and ATP7A phenotype.
Menkes disease reflects impaired copper transport/efflux rather than excessive intestinal copper absorption.
key_expl: ATP7A loss prevents normal copper trafficking and efflux from enterocytes, causing intestinal copper trapping and systemic copper deficiency. Reduced activity of copper-dependent enzymes contributes to the neurologic, connective-tissue, and hair abnormalities.
objective: Explain Menkes disease as ATP7A-dependent failure of intestinal copper efflux and systemic copper delivery.
